finite_smoke.asserts: For an integer $K\ge2$, let the label set be $\mathcal Y=\{1,\ldots,K\}$ and let $\Delta_K=\{q\in[0,1]^K:\sum_{j=1}^Kq_j=1\}$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

derivations.claim: If $Z$ has finite range $z_1,\ldots,z_m\in C$ with probabilities $p_1,\ldots,p_m$, then each coordinate of $Z$ is a nonnegative simple function, so [F3] gives $\mathbb E Z=\sum_i p_i z_i$, a convex combination in $C$. The real finite-range random variable $\psi(Z)$ is integrable. Its positive and negative parts are nonnegative simple functions, so applying [F3] to each and subtracting their finite expectations gives $\mathbb E[\psi(Z)]=\sum_i p_i\psi(z_i)$. Joint convexity now proves $\psi(\mathbb E Z)\le\mathbb E[\psi(Z)]$ by induction on the number of positive weights: combine the first $m-1$ points into their normalized convex average, apply the induction hypothesis, then apply two-point convexity with weights $1-p_m$ and $p_m$.

For $n\ge1$ set $D_n=\{(m_1/n,\ldots,m_K/n):m_i\in\mathbb N_0,\sum_i m_i=n\}\subseteq\Delta_K$. This is a finite set with a canonical lexicographic order. For $p\in\Delta_K$, put $m_i=\lfloor np_i\rfloor$ for $i<K$ and $m_K=n-\sum_{i<K}m_i$. Then $m_K\ge0$, the coordinates sum to $n$, and the first $K-1$ coordinate errors are below $1/n$ while the last is below $(K-1)/n$. Thus some $q\in D_n$ has $\|p-q\|_2<\sqrt{K(K-1)}/n$. The product grid $D_n\times D_n$ therefore approximates every point of $C$ within $2K/n$. List its finitely many points canonically as $c_{n,1},\ldots,c_{n,m_n}$. Their relative open balls of radius $2K/n$ cover $C$, and the cells obtained by removing all earlier balls from each ball are Borel in the stated subspace sigma-algebra. Assign each point to its first covering ball; replacing $Z$ on each cell by its center defines a measurable finite-range $Z_n\in C$ with $\|Z_n-Z\|_2<2K/n$ everywhere. The grid, order and assignment are explicit, so no choice axiom is used.

Step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E Z_n\in C$ for every $n$. Each coordinate of $Z_n$ and $Z$ is bounded by $1$, so dominated convergence [F4] gives $\mathbb E Z_n\to\mathbb E Z$ coordinatewise; because the coordinate constraints defining $C$ are closed, $\mathbb E Z\in C$.

By [F2], $\psi$ is uniformly continuous on $C$. Choose $\delta>0$ so that points within distance $\delta$ have $\psi$-values within $1$, and then choose $n$ with $2K/n<\delta$. The finite grid in step 1.2 is a $\delta$-net, so $|\psi(z)|\le1+\max_{c\in D_n\times D_n}|\psi(c)|$ for every $z\in C$. This is a common finite bound. Since $\|Z_n-Z\|_2\to0$, continuity gives $\psi(Z_n)\to\psi(Z)$ pointwise; [F4] then gives $\mathbb E\psi(Z_n)\to\mathbb E\psi(Z)$.
Applying step 1.1 to each $Z_n$ gives $\psi(\mathbb E Z_n)\le\mathbb E\psi(Z_n)$. By continuity of $\psi$ and steps 2.1 and 2.2, taking limits proves $\psi(\mathbb E Z)\le\mathbb E\psi(Z)$.

$$(a^x)'=a^x\log a.$$
For $\alpha\in\mathbb R$, the function $x\mapsto x^\alpha$ is continuous and differentiable on $(0,\infty)$, with

If $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is twice differentiable on an open interval, then $f$ is convex if and only if $f''(x)\ge0$ for every $x\in I$.

For the supplementary zero-base convention, define $0^x:=0$ when $x>0$.

For $a,b>0$ and $r,s\in\mathbb R$,
$$a^{r+s}=a^ra^s,\qquad (ab)^r=a^rb^r,\qquad (a/b)^r=a^r/b^r,\qquad (a^r)^s=a^{rs}.$$

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]), let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ interior to $I$
([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]). The words
*nondecreasing*, *increasing*, *nonincreasing* and *decreasing* are those of
[[def-monotone-function]], in which *increasing* is the strict notion.

1. If $f'(x) \ge 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nondecreasing on $I$.
2. If $f'(x) > 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is increasing on
   $I$.
3. If $f'(x) \le 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is
   nonincreasing on $I$.
4. If $f'(x) < 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is decreasing on
   $I$.

Conversely, with no continuity hypothesis and no hypothesis at any other point:

5. If $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ is nondecreasing on $I$ and differentiable at a
   point $c \in I$ that is a limit point of $I$, then $f'(c) \ge 0$; if $f$ is
   nonincreasing and differentiable at such a $c$, then $f'(c) \le 0$.

**No strict converse is claimed here, and none is true.** Claim 5 gives the
weak inequality only, and it cannot be improved: an increasing function may have
a vanishing derivative at a point. That failure is recorded separately, as a
false statement later on this page, with its witness worked out on the companion
page. Reading claim 2 backwards is the single most common misuse of this
theorem, and this statement does not license it.

**Claims 1 to 4 need the interval; claim 5 does not.** The forward direction
runs through the mean value theorem on a segment joining two points of $I$, so
order-convexity is essential. Claim 5 is a statement about one point and uses
only that the difference quotients have a constant sign.

Let $K\ge2$, let $Y$ be a random variable into the finite label set $\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with its full power-set sigma-algebra on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, and let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_K):\Omega\to\Delta_K$ be a measurable forecast, where $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_jp_j=1\}$. The forecast is **fully reliable** if for every label $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}G_j].$$
It is **classwise calibrated** if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G_j\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G_j\in B\}}G_j].$$
For the **top-confidence calibration** condition, define $C=\max_jG_j$ and $\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=C\}$, so ties go to the smallest label. The forecast is top-confidence calibrated if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
A measurable function $r:\Delta_K\to\Delta_K$ is a **calibration function** for $G$ if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}r_j(G)].$$
When such a function is supplied and $d:\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\to[0,+\infty)$ is measurable, the **expected calibration error with discrepancy $d$** is $\eta_d=\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.
Assume AC. For every real integrable $X$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and every sub-sigma-algebra $\mathcal G$, a conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$ exists.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.
If $Y,Z$ are conditional-expectation versions of the same real integrable $X$ given $\mathcal G$, then $Y=Z$ almost surely.

Let $f,g\in L^1(\mu)$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $f=g$ almost everywhere;
2. for every measurable $A$,
   $$\int_A f\,d\mu=\int_A g\,d\mu.$$

For integrable real or complex $h$, the notation in condition 2 means
$\int_A h\,d\mu:=\int h\chi_A\,d\mu$; the product is integrable because
$|h\chi_A|\le|h|$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}G_j].$$
It is **classwise calibrated** if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,

To apply the Bayes-risk interface to the original joint law, let $\pi_j=P(Y=j)$. For $\pi_j>0$, define $K_j(A)=P(X\in A,Y=j)/\pi_j$ on feature events $A$; for $\pi_j=0$, set $K_j=P_X$. Let $K\ge2$, let $Y$ be a random variable into the finite label set $\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with its full power-set sigma-algebra on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, and let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_K):\Omega\to\Delta_K$ be a measurable forecast, where $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_jp_j=1\}$. The forecast is **fully reliable** if for every label $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}G_j].$$
It is **classwise calibrated** if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G_j\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G_j\in B\}}G_j].$$
For the **top-confidence calibration** condition, define $C=\max_jG_j$ and $\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=C\}$, so ties go to the smallest label. The forecast is top-confidence calibrated if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
A measurable function $r:\Delta_K\to\Delta_K$ is a **calibration function** for $G$ if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}r_j(G)].$$
When such a function is supplied and $d:\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\to[0,+\infty)$ is measurable, the **expected calibration error with discrepancy $d$** is $\eta_d=\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

For an integer $K\ge2$, let $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_{j=1}^Kp_j=1\}\subset\mathbb R^K$ with its subspace Borel sigma-algebra, and let $C=\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\subset\mathbb R^{2K}$ with its subspace Borel sigma-algebra. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $Z=(U,V):\Omega\to C$ be measurable, and let $\psi:C\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and jointly convex, meaning $\psi(\lambda z+(1-\lambda)w)\le\lambda\psi(z)+(1-\lambda)\psi(w)$ for all $z,w\in C$ and $\lambda\in[0,1]$. Define $\mathbb E Z$ coordinatewise. Then $\mathbb E Z=(\mathbb E U,\mathbb E V)\in C$ and
$$\psi(\mathbb E U,\mathbb E V)\le\mathbb E[\psi(U,V)].$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be an independent family of random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. For each $i$, let
$g_i:(S_i,\Sigma_i)\to(T_i,\mathcal T_i)$ be measurable. Then the family
$(g_i\circ X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent.
For IID real $(X_n)_{n\ge1}$ with $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, $S_n/n\to\mu=\mathbb EX_1$ almost surely.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$. A von Neumann natural is the set of its
predecessors, $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]), so it can be
used directly as an index set. Define

$$\mathbb{R}^n := \{\, x : x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\},$$

and write $x_k$ for $x(k)$, $k < n$. Two elements of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are equal
exactly when they agree at every $k < n$, functions being equal when they have
the same values. For $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^n$ put

$$d_1(x,y) := \sum_{k<n} |x_k - y_k|, \qquad d_2(x,y) := \sqrt{\ \sum_{k<n} (x_k - y_k)^2\ }, \qquad d_\infty(x,y) := \max\{\, |x_k - y_k| : k < n \,\}.$$

All three are well defined: the finite sums are those of [[def-finite-sum]]; the
sum of squares is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]], [[lem-of-square-positive]])
so it has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]); and
$\{|x_k - y_k| : k < n\}$ is a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$, because
$n \ge 1$, so it has a maximum ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**Then $d_1$, $d_2$ and $d_\infty$ are metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$**
([[def-metric-space]]).

**Why $n \ge 1$.** For $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^0$ has exactly one element,
the empty function, and $d_1$ and $d_2$ are the empty sum $0$ and its root; but
$d_\infty$ would be the maximum of the empty set, which does not exist. The
hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is therefore not decoration, and it is carried by every
statement about $d_\infty$ in this library.

derivations.claim: Fix a partition $\mathcal P$. For every bin $B$ and each coordinate, the variables $\mathbf1_{\{G_i\in B\}}$, $\mathbf1_{\{G_i\in B\}}(V_i)_j$, and $\mathbf1_{\{G_i\in B\}}(G_i)_j$ are bounded iid real variables: the same measurable coordinate map is applied to each iid pair, so the outputs have the same law by taking preimages, and their independence follows from [F3]. Their sample averages therefore converge almost surely to their expectations. On the event $P(G\in B)>0$, division by $N_B/n\to P(G\in B)$ gives convergence of the bin means to $\mathbb E[V\mid G\in B]$ and $\mathbb E[G\mid G\in B]$. On a zero-probability bin every sample has count zero almost surely. Since the partition and label set are finite, these convergences hold together almost surely; continuity of $d$ then gives $\widehat E_{n,\mathcal P}\to E_{\mathcal P}$. By [F1], $\mathbb E[V\mid G\in B]=\mathbb E[r(G)\mid G\in B]$ coordinatewise.

Let $\delta_m$ be the maximum Euclidean diameter of a cell of $\mathcal P_m$. For any fixed $v\in\Delta_K$, the function $\psi(u,w)=\|u-w\|_2$ is continuous and jointly convex: the metric triangle inequality gives continuity in $(u,w)$, and
$$\|\lambda(u-w)+(1-\lambda)(u'-w')\|_2\le\lambda\|u-w\|_2+(1-\lambda)\|u'-w'\|_2$$
for $0\le\lambda\le1$ by the triangle inequality and homogeneity in [F5]. For a positive-probability bin $B$, define $P_B(A)=P(A\cap\{G\in B\})/P(G\in B)$. If $G(\omega)\in B$, apply [F2] under $P_B$ to the simplex pair $(G,G(\omega))$. It gives $\|\mathbb E[G\mid G\in B]-G(\omega)\|_2\le\mathbb E[\|G-G(\omega)\|_2\mid G\in B]\le\delta_m$. Apply the same argument to $(r(G),r(G(\omega)))$ to obtain $\|\mathbb E[r(G)\mid G\in B]-r(G(\omega))\|_2\le L\delta_m$. Thus the Euclidean distance between the ordered pairs is at most $\sqrt{1+L^2}\,\delta_m\le(1+L)\delta_m$. By [F4], $d$ is uniformly continuous on the compact product simplex, so the absolute difference between the bin value and $d(r(G(\omega)),G(\omega))$ is bounded by a modulus tending to zero with $\delta_m$, uniformly over all bins and $\omega$. Integrating over bins yields $E_{\mathcal P_m}\to\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

For the underestimation conclusion assume additionally that $d$ is jointly convex. For each positive-probability bin define the conditional probability measure $P_B(A)=P(A\cap\{G\in B\})/P(G\in B)$. Under $P_B$, the pair $(r(G),G)$ takes values in $\Delta_K\times\Delta_K$. Apply [F2] to $\psi=d$ and multiply by $P(G\in B)$ to obtain $P(G\in B)d\!\left(\mathbb E[r(G)\mid G\in B],\mathbb E[G\mid G\in B]\right)\le\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}d(r(G),G)].$ Summing over the partition proves $E_{\mathcal P}\le\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

For each fixed $m$, step 1.1 gives the almost-sure limit in $n$. There are countably many $m$, so the intersection of these probability-one events still has probability one; step 1.2 then gives the iterated limit as stated. itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

citations.quote: Assume AC. Let a finite-label supervised prediction problem have measurable instance space $(\mathsf X,\Sigma_X)$ and finite labels $\mathcal Y=\{y_1,\ldots,y_K\}$ with the full power-set sigma-algebra, where $K\ge2$. Identify label $y_j$ with its index $j$ when applying numbered-label calibration, so forecast coordinate $j$ always represents the event $Y=y_j$. For every measurable feature $T:\mathsf X\to(\mathsf Z,\Sigma_Z)$, there is a measurable $\eta_T:\mathsf Z\to\Delta_K$ such that $G=\eta_T(T(X))$ is a conditional class-probability forecast given $T(X)$ and is fully reliable. This includes the identity feature and a constant feature.

Let $K\ge2$, let $Y$ be a random variable into the finite label set $\{1,\ldots,K\}$ with its full power-set sigma-algebra on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, and let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_K):\Omega\to\Delta_K$ be a measurable forecast, where $\Delta_K=\{p\in[0,1]^K:\sum_jp_j=1\}$. The forecast is **fully reliable** if for every label $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}G_j].$$
It is **classwise calibrated** if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G_j\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G_j\in B\}}G_j].$$
For the **top-confidence calibration** condition, define $C=\max_jG_j$ and $\widehat Y=\min\{j:G_j=C\}$, so ties go to the smallest label. The forecast is top-confidence calibrated if for every Borel set $B\subseteq[0,1]$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=\widehat Y,\ C\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{C\in B\}}C].$$
A measurable function $r:\Delta_K\to\Delta_K$ is a **calibration function** for $G$ if for every $j$ and every Borel set $B\subseteq\Delta_K$,
$$\mathbb P(Y=j,\ G\in B)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{G\in B\}}r_j(G)].$$
When such a function is supplied and $d:\Delta_K\times\Delta_K\to[0,+\infty)$ is measurable, the **expected calibration error with discrepancy $d$** is $\eta_d=\mathbb E[d(r(G),G)]$.

derivations.claim: The probability of $T=u$ is $2/3$, and the conditional probability of $Y=1$ there is $(0.1+0.9)/2=0.5$; at $T=v$ it is $0.75$. Thus the forecast is exactly the conditional label distribution given $T$, and [F1] implies full reliability. Directly, each forecast value identifies $T$, so the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $G=(0.5,0.5)$ is $(0.5,0.5)$ and given $G=(0.75,0.25)$ is $(0.75,0.25)$, which is [F2].

The original feature values $a$ and $b$ have different conditional label laws, with success probabilities $0.1$ and $0.9$, but both map to the same forecast. Hence observing the forecast does not determine which of those feature values occurred, so the forecast discards information about $X$ while remaining calibrated.

finite_smoke.asserts: Give $X\in\{a,b,c\}$ and the binary label $Y\in\{1,2\}$ their full power-set sigma-algebras. Let $X$ be uniform on $\{a,b,c\}$ and let the conditional probabilities be $P(Y=1\mid X=a)=0.1$, $P(Y=1\mid X=b)=0.9$, and $P(Y=1\mid X=c)=0.75$. Coarsen the feature by $T(a)=T(b)=u$ and $T(c)=v$, and forecast $G=(P(Y=1\mid T),P(Y=2\mid T))$. Then $G(a)=G(b)=(0.5,0.5)$ and $G(c)=(0.75,0.25)$. This forecast is fully reliable, although it cannot distinguish $a$ from $b$, whose conditional label laws differ.
